group.title: Business and finance
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To get or buy something, especially a company or an asset.
examples: The firm plans to {acquire} a smaller competitor.
wrong: A company acquires another company by selling it for nothing.

words.meaning: The regular costs of running a business, such as rent and power.
examples: High {overhead} made it hard for the cafe to make money.
wrong: Overhead is the extra money a customer gives as a tip.

words.meaning: Something of value that a person or company owns.
examples: The building is the company’s biggest {asset}.
wrong: An asset is a debt that you must pay back next week.

words.meaning: A debt or legal duty that a person or company must pay or meet.
examples: The loan is a {liability} on the company’s books.
wrong: A liability is a valuable thing that makes the company richer.

words.meaning: A period of three months in a company’s financial year.
examples: Sales rose sharply in the fourth {quarter}.
wrong: A quarter is a meeting that lasts for fifteen minutes.

words.meaning: A standard used to compare how well something is doing.
examples: The industry average is our {benchmark} for customer service.
wrong: A benchmark is a bench in front of the office.

words.meaning: The difference between the cost of something and the price it sells for.
examples: The shop has a low {margin} on each sale.
wrong: A margin is the blank space where you sign a contract.

words.meaning: Something that encourages a person to act in a certain way.
examples: The bonus is a strong {incentive} to finish early.
wrong: An incentive is a punishment for finishing early.

words.meaning: The process of finding and buying goods or services for an organization.
examples: {Procurement} checks every supplier before a contract is signed.
wrong: Procurement is the process of selling goods to customers.

words.meaning: Following the rules, laws or standards that apply to you.
examples: The audit checks the firm’s {compliance} with safety rules.
wrong: Compliance means choosing to ignore the rules.

words.meaning: Able to grow bigger without a large increase in cost or effort.
examples: The software is {scalable}, so it can serve a million users.
wrong: A scalable plan only works for exactly one customer.

words.meaning: To use something you have in order to get a better result.
examples: We can {leverage} our reputation to win new clients.
wrong: You leverage an advantage by throwing it away.

words.meaning: To make a major change in the direction of a business or plan.
examples: The startup had to {pivot} when its first product failed.
wrong: A company pivots by doing exactly the same thing forever.

words.meaning: A new company, often in technology, that is just beginning to grow.
examples: She left her job to launch a {startup}.
wrong: A startup is a company that has existed for a hundred years.

words.meaning: A regular payment that gives you access to a service or product.
examples: I pay a monthly {subscription} for the news app.
wrong: A subscription is a single payment that you can never cancel or repeat.

words.meaning: The selling of goods to the public, usually in shops or online.
examples: She works in {retail} and serves customers all day.
wrong: Retail means selling goods only to other companies in huge amounts.

words.meaning: A share of a company’s profit paid to the people who own its shares.
examples: The company paid a {dividend} to every shareholder.
wrong: A dividend is a fee that a customer pays to join a company.

words.meaning: The movement of money into and out of a business.
examples: Late payments caused a {cash flow} problem.
wrong: Cash flow is the total number of workers a company employs.

words.meaning: The total amount of money that a person or organization spends.
examples: Government {expenditure} rose again this year.
wrong: Expenditure is the money that a company earns from sales.

words.meaning: A general rise in prices over time.
examples: {Inflation} made groceries more expensive.
wrong: Inflation is a fall in the prices of all goods.

words.meaning: A period when a country’s economy shrinks and many people lose jobs.
examples: Many shops closed during the {recession}.
wrong: A recession is a period when every business grows quickly.

words.meaning: A tax on goods that come into a country.
examples: The {tariff} made imported cars more expensive.
wrong: A tariff is a discount that a shop gives to a regular customer.

words.meaning: The right to use a company’s name and methods, or a business run under that right.
examples: She bought a {franchise} of a famous burger chain.
wrong: A franchise is a business that has no name and no customers.

words.meaning: A load of goods sent from one place to another.
examples: The {shipment} arrived at the port on Monday.
wrong: A shipment is a meeting where the managers vote.

words.meaning: The list of employees and the money paid to them.
examples: The company has fifty people on its {payroll}.
wrong: Payroll is the money that customers pay to a company.

words.meaning: A name and image that make a product easy to recognize.
examples: The {brand} is known for its simple design.
wrong: A brand is a mistake in a company’s accounts.

words.meaning: A person who buys goods or services for their own use.
examples: Each {consumer} has a right to clear prices.
wrong: A consumer is a company that makes and sells the goods.
